title: IBPS SO IT Mains – Day 1: DBMS
answer_format: answer is the option letter a–e mapping to options[0]–options[4]

questions.question: In the three-schema architecture, which level describes how data is physically stored on disk?
questions.explanation: Internal (physical) level = storage structures. External = user views; Conceptual = whole logical structure.

questions.question: Adding a new column to a table without having to rewrite existing application programs is an example of:
questions.explanation: Changing the conceptual schema without affecting views/apps = logical data independence (harder to achieve than physical).

questions.question: An employee's age, computed from their date of birth, is an example of which attribute type?
questions.explanation: Derived attributes are computed from stored ones (Age from DOB).

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) has only one candidate key, {A}. How many super keys does R have?
questions.explanation: With n attributes and one candidate key of k attributes: 2^(n-k) = 2^4 = 16. (Harder than typical IBPS level.)

questions.question: Which statement about a foreign key is FALSE?
options: It must reference a primary or unique key
It must be unique within the child table
questions.explanation: A foreign key may repeat and may be NULL. It doesn't have to be unique.

questions.question: Student and Course have an M:N relationship 'Enrolls'. What is the minimum number of tables needed to map this to a relational schema?
questions.explanation: Two entity tables plus one table for the M:N relationship = 3.

questions.question: Which operation can never violate referential integrity?
options: Inserting a row into the child table
Deleting a row from the parent table
Updating the PK in the parent table
Inserting a row into the parent table
Updating the FK in the child table
questions.explanation: Inserting into the parent (and deleting from the child) can never break referential integrity.

questions.question: The number of tuples in a relation is called its:
questions.explanation: Cardinality = rows. Degree (arity) = columns.

questions.question: In the EER model, which concept treats a relationship set as an entity so that it can take part in another relationship?
questions.explanation: Aggregation treats a relationship as a higher-level entity.

questions.question: Which ACID property ensures that the changes made by a committed transaction survive a system crash?
questions.explanation: 'After commit' + 'crash' = Durability.

questions.question: Which SQL command removes all rows from a table but keeps its structure, and cannot be used with a WHERE clause?
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE removes all rows, keeps structure, no WHERE. DELETE can filter; DROP removes the table.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about a primary key is incorrect?
options: A table can have more than one primary key
It can be made of multiple columns
It is chosen from the candidate keys
questions.explanation: A table has exactly one primary key (which may be composite).

questions.question: Which condition selects employees whose name starts with 'S' and is exactly 5 characters long?
questions.explanation: 'S' plus four '_' (each exactly one character) = 5 characters.

questions.question: A relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and:
options: Every determinant is a candidate key
It has only one candidate key
No non-prime attribute is partially dependent on any candidate key
questions.explanation: 2NF removes partial dependencies.

questions.question: Which type of lock can be held on the same data item by multiple transactions at the same time?
questions.explanation: Only S + S is compatible.

questions.question: Which join returns all rows from the left table plus the matching rows from the right table, with NULLs where there is no match?
questions.explanation: LEFT OUTER JOIN keeps every left row.

questions.question: Which of the following is a DCL command?
questions.explanation: DCL = GRANT, REVOKE. COMMIT/SAVEPOINT = TCL; ALTER = DDL; MERGE = DML.

questions.question: Which SQL clause filters groups after aggregation has been applied?
questions.explanation: HAVING filters groups. WHERE filters rows; GROUP BY only forms groups.

questions.question: In MongoDB, data is stored as:
questions.explanation: MongoDB is a document store using BSON (binary JSON).

questions.question: A customer transfers ₹5,000. The amount is debited from their account, but a power failure stops it from being credited to the receiver. Which ACID property is violated?
questions.explanation: Failure in the middle = partial update = Atomicity (all or nothing).

questions.question: Which of the following is a graph-based NoSQL database?
questions.explanation: Neo4j = graph. Cassandra/HBase = column-family, MongoDB = document, Redis = key-value.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: WHERE can directly use aggregate functions such as SUM()
GROUP BY is evaluated before HAVING
ORDER BY is evaluated after SELECT
questions.explanation: WHERE can't use aggregates; that is HAVING's job. ORDER BY really does run after SELECT.

questions.question: Transitive dependency is removed in which normal form?
questions.explanation: 3NF removes transitive dependency; 2NF removes partial dependency.

questions.question: Transaction T1 holds an exclusive lock on data item A. Transaction T2 now requests a shared lock on A. What happens?
options: T2 must wait until T1 releases the lock
T1's lock is converted to a shared lock
questions.explanation: X is incompatible with everything, so T2 waits.

questions.question: Which of the following is a TCL command?
questions.explanation: TCL = COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT.

questions.question: Which SQL operator checks whether a subquery returns at least one row?
questions.explanation: EXISTS is true if the subquery returns any row.

questions.question: Which join returns the Cartesian product of two tables?
questions.explanation: CROSS JOIN = every row paired with every row.

questions.question: A relation in which every determinant is a candidate key is in:
questions.explanation: That is the definition of BCNF.

questions.question: Which MongoDB feature distributes data across multiple servers for horizontal scaling?
questions.explanation: Sharding = horizontal scaling. Replication = availability.

questions.question: Which relational algebra operation returns the tuples that are in R1 but not in R2?
questions.explanation: R1 − R2 = set difference.

questions.question: Which SQL operator combines the results of two queries and removes duplicate rows?
questions.explanation: UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them.

questions.question: In MySQL, which query returns the 3rd highest salary?
questions.explanation: LIMIT offset, count. nth highest = LIMIT n-1, 1.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about TRUNCATE is incorrect?
options: It removes all rows from a table
It is classified as a DDL command
It is generally faster than DELETE
It fires row-level DELETE triggers for each row
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE deallocates pages; it doesn't fire DELETE triggers.

questions.question: In Tuple Relational Calculus, what does the expression {t | Student(t) ∧ t.marks > 80} return?
options: Only the marks attribute of all students
All tuples of Student with marks greater than 80
All students with marks less than or equal to 80
The total marks of all students
questions.explanation: {t | P(t)} returns whole tuples satisfying the condition.

questions.question: Which concurrency control protocol guarantees serializability but can still lead to deadlock?
questions.explanation: Basic 2PL is serializable but can deadlock. Timestamp ordering and tree protocol are deadlock-free.

questions.question: Which constraint ensures that the value of Age stays between 18 and 60?
questions.explanation: CHECK enforces a condition on values.

questions.question: A virtual table defined by the result of a SELECT query is called a:
questions.explanation: A view stores only the query, not the data.

questions.question: Which window function assigns ranks to tied values and then leaves gaps in the ranking sequence?
questions.explanation: RANK: 1,1,3. DENSE_RANK: 1,1,2. ROW_NUMBER: 1,2,3.

questions.question: Which key enforces uniqueness but still allows NULL values?
questions.explanation: UNIQUE allows NULL; PRIMARY KEY doesn't.

questions.question: Which statement about basic Two-Phase Locking (2PL) is correct?
options: It guarantees conflict serializability but can lead to deadlock
It releases locks only at commit
questions.explanation: Basic 2PL: serializable, but deadlock and cascading rollback are possible.

questions.question: Which variant of 2PL is free from deadlock?
questions.explanation: Conservative 2PL acquires all locks before starting, so no deadlock.

questions.question: Under the Wait-Die scheme, T1 (TS = 5) requests a lock held by T2 (TS = 10). What happens?
questions.explanation: Smaller TS = older. In Wait-Die, an older requester waits.

questions.question: A DBMS detects deadlock using:
options: A precedence graph without a cycle
A wait-for graph containing a cycle
questions.explanation: Cycle in the wait-for graph = deadlock.

questions.question: In Strict 2PL, which locks are held until the transaction commits or aborts?
questions.explanation: Strict = exclusive locks till commit. Rigorous = all locks till commit.

questions.question: T2 reads a value written by T1 before T1 commits, and then T1 aborts. Which problem has occurred?
questions.explanation: Reading uncommitted data = dirty read.

questions.question: What does the Thomas Write Rule do?
options: Aborts the transaction on every conflict
Ignores obsolete write operations instead of rolling back
Converts shared locks to exclusive locks
questions.explanation: If TS(T) < W-TS(X), the outdated write is ignored.

questions.question: If the precedence graph of a schedule contains a cycle, the schedule is:
questions.explanation: Precedence graph cycle = not conflict serializable. (Wait-for graph cycle = deadlock.)

questions.question: Concurrency control mechanisms primarily ensure which ACID property?
questions.explanation: Concurrency control = Isolation.

questions.question: Which of the following ensures that cascading rollbacks never occur?
questions.explanation: Strict 2PL holds X locks till commit, so nobody reads uncommitted data.

questions.question: In Rigorous 2PL, which locks are held until the transaction commits?
questions.explanation: Rigorous = all locks till commit.

questions.question: Under Wound-Wait, T1 (TS = 5) requests a lock held by T2 (TS = 10). What happens?
options: The lock is granted to both
questions.explanation: T1 is older; in Wound-Wait the older requester wounds (rolls back) the younger holder.

questions.question: Schedules produced using the Thomas Write Rule are:
questions.explanation: Thomas Write Rule allows view-serializable (not necessarily conflict-serializable) schedules.

questions.question: In a precedence graph, an edge Ti → Tj is drawn when:
options: Ti waits for a lock held by Tj
An operation of Ti conflicts with, and comes before, an operation of Tj
Ti and Tj read the same item
Tj has an older timestamp than Ti
questions.explanation: Option (a) describes a wait-for graph edge.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a checkpoint in log-based recovery?
options: To reduce the amount of log scanned during recovery
questions.explanation: Checkpoints limit how much log must be scanned after a crash.

questions.question: After a crash, the log contains both <Start T1> and <Commit T1>. During recovery, T1 is:
questions.explanation: Commit present = redo. No commit = undo.

questions.question: Which statement about shadow paging is correct?
options: It keeps a current page table and a shadow page table, and doesn't need an undo/redo log
It is used for deadlock detection
It maintains a single page table
It is a concurrency control protocol
questions.explanation: Shadow paging uses two page tables and copy-on-write.

questions.question: T2 reads a value written by T1, and T2 commits before T1 commits. This schedule is:
questions.explanation: If T1 later aborts, the committed T2 can't be undone.

questions.question: Which isolation level prevents dirty reads but still allows unrepeatable reads?
questions.explanation: Read Committed blocks only dirty reads.

questions.question: Which pair of operations does NOT conflict?
questions.explanation: Two reads never conflict; at least one must be a write.

questions.question: Under Wound-Wait, T2 (TS = 20) requests a lock held by T1 (TS = 10). What happens?
questions.explanation: T2 is younger; in Wound-Wait a younger requester waits.

questions.question: In both Wait-Die and Wound-Wait, which transaction is rolled back?
options: Always the one holding the lock
Always the one requesting the lock
questions.explanation: Younger is always the victim in both schemes.

questions.question: In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti → Tj means:
options: Ti conflicts with and precedes Tj
Ti and Tj hold shared locks on the same item
Ti is waiting for Tj to release a lock
questions.explanation: Wait-for graph edges show who is waiting for whom.

questions.question: After a crash, the log contains <Start T2> but no <Commit T2>. During recovery, T2 is:
questions.explanation: No commit = undo.

questions.question: A schedule is recoverable if:
options: All transactions run one after another
Each transaction commits only after every transaction it read from has committed
questions.explanation: Reader commits after writer.

questions.question: Which isolation level prevents dirty reads, unrepeatable reads and phantom reads?
questions.explanation: Serializable blocks all three.

questions.question: Checkpoints in a DBMS mainly help to:
options: Reduce recovery time after a crash
questions.explanation: Less log to scan = faster recovery.

questions.question: In a cascadeless schedule:
options: Every transaction holds all locks until commit
questions.explanation: Cascadeless = read only committed data.

questions.question: Under the Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) rule:
options: The log record is written to stable storage before the data page is written
The data page is written before the log record
Logs are written only at checkpoints
Logs are written only after commit
No log is needed for recovery
questions.explanation: Log first, then data.

questions.question: Which recovery technique keeps two page tables and does not need undo/redo logs?
questions.explanation: Shadow paging.

questions.question: An attribute whose value is calculated from another attribute is called a:
questions.explanation: Derived (e.g. Age from DOB).

questions.question: Which statement about super keys and candidate keys is incorrect?
options: Every candidate key is a super key
Every super key is a candidate key
A candidate key is a minimal super key
A relation can have more than one candidate key
The primary key is chosen from the candidate keys
questions.explanation: Super keys may contain extra attributes, so not all are candidate keys.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a domain constraint?
options: It specifies the set of allowed values for an attribute
It ensures that every row has a unique key
It prevents NULL values in every column
questions.explanation: Domain constraint = allowed values for a column.

questions.question: Partial dependency is removed when a relation is converted to which normal form?
questions.explanation: 2NF removes partial dependency.

questions.question: Which referential action sets the foreign key in the child rows to NULL when the parent row is deleted?
questions.explanation: SET NULL.

questions.question: A weak entity is uniquely identified by:
options: The owner entity's primary key combined with its partial key
questions.explanation: Owner PK + partial key (discriminator).

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C) has the functional dependencies A → B and B → C, and its only candidate key is A. What is the highest normal form R satisfies?
questions.explanation: B → C is transitive (non-prime → non-prime), so 3NF fails. No partial dependency, so 2NF.

questions.question: Which key can never contain a NULL value?
questions.explanation: Entity integrity: PK can't be NULL.

questions.question: A relation is in BCNF if, for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y:
questions.explanation: BCNF: every determinant is a super key.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about 3NF is true?
options: A table is in 3NF if all of its attributes are atomic
A table is in 3NF if it has only one candidate key
A table is in 3NF if it is in 2NF and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on any candidate key
A table is in 3NF if every determinant is a foreign key
A table is in 3NF if it has no multivalued dependency
questions.explanation: 3NF = 2NF + no transitive dependency.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has candidate key {A, B} and the functional dependency A → C. What is the highest normal form R satisfies?
questions.explanation: A is part of the key and determines non-prime C: partial dependency, so only 1NF.

questions.question: A relation is in 1NF when:
options: Every determinant is a candidate key
Every attribute contains only atomic values
questions.explanation: 1NF = atomic values.

questions.question: Which of the following can contain both duplicate values and NULLs?
questions.explanation: Foreign keys can repeat and be NULL.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C) has the functional dependencies AB → C and C → B. Its candidate keys are AB and AC. What is the highest normal form R satisfies?
questions.explanation: All attributes are prime, so 3NF holds. C → B has a non-super-key determinant, so BCNF fails.

questions.question: If two attributes P and Q satisfy both P → Q and Q → P, they show:
questions.explanation: Mutual functional dependency (PYQ 2023).

questions.question: Attributes that are part of some candidate key are called:
questions.explanation: Prime attributes.

questions.question: The entity integrity constraint states that:
options: A foreign key must match a primary key
A primary key cannot be NULL
Values must belong to a domain
Every table must have an index
questions.explanation: Option (a) is referential integrity.

questions.question: Which normal form deals with multivalued dependencies?
questions.explanation: 4NF removes MVDs; 5NF removes join dependencies.

questions.question: A functional dependency X → Y is called trivial when:
options: Y is a subset of X
questions.explanation: Trivial: Y ⊆ X, e.g. AB → A.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has the functional dependencies A → B, B → C and C → D, and its only candidate key is A. What is the highest normal form R satisfies?
questions.explanation: Single-attribute key, so no partial dependency (2NF). B → C is transitive, so not 3NF.

questions.question: Which constraint requires a foreign key value to either match an existing primary key value in the referenced table or be NULL?
questions.explanation: Referential integrity.

questions.question: Which of the following functional dependencies is trivial?
questions.explanation: A ⊆ AB.

questions.question: Relation R(X, Y, Z) has the functional dependencies XY → Z and Z → X. Its candidate keys are XY and YZ. What is the highest normal form R satisfies?
questions.explanation: All attributes prime, so 3NF. Z → X: Z isn't a super key, so not BCNF.

questions.question: Every relation that has only two attributes is always in:
questions.explanation: Any FD in a 2-attribute relation has a key as determinant.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: Every relation in BCNF is also in 3NF
Every relation in 3NF is also in BCNF
Every relation in 3NF is also in 2NF
questions.explanation: 3NF does not guarantee BCNF.

questions.question: Given the functional dependencies A → B, B → C and C → D, what is the closure of A (A⁺)?
questions.explanation: A → B → C → D, plus A itself.

questions.question: A decomposition of relation R into R1 and R2 is lossless if:
options: R1 ∩ R2 is a super key of R1 or of R2
R1 and R2 have no common attributes
R1 and R2 each have exactly one attribute
R1 is a subset of R2
questions.explanation: The common attributes must be a key of at least one side.

questions.question: Deleting a row unintentionally removes other useful information stored in the same row. This is called:
questions.explanation: Deletion anomaly.

questions.question: A candidate key that is not chosen as the primary key is called a(n):
questions.explanation: Alternate key.

questions.question: Which query selects employees whose name contains 'a' and whose city is not Delhi?
options: SELECT * FROM Emp WHERE Name = '%a%' AND City != 'Delhi';
SELECT * FROM Emp WHERE Name LIKE '%a%' AND City NOT LIKE 'Delhi';
SELECT * FROM Emp WHERE Name IN '%a%' AND City NOT IN 'Delhi';
SELECT * FROM Emp WHERE Name LIKE '%a%' OR City NOT LIKE 'Delhi';
SELECT * FROM Emp WHERE Name NOT LIKE '%a%' AND City LIKE 'Delhi';
questions.explanation: Patterns need LIKE, and both conditions need AND.

questions.question: Which statement about DELETE and TRUNCATE is correct?
options: DELETE is DML and can use a WHERE clause; TRUNCATE is DDL and removes all rows
TRUNCATE can use a WHERE clause
questions.explanation: DELETE = DML with WHERE; TRUNCATE = DDL, all rows.

questions.question: In MySQL, what does SELECT INSTR('banking', 'k'); return?
questions.explanation: SQL positions are 1-based: b1 a2 n3 k4.

questions.question: What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column_name)?
options: COUNT(column_name) counts duplicate values only once
COUNT(*) works only together with GROUP BY
COUNT(column_name) ignores NULL values in that column
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs.

questions.question: Which query lists the departments that have more than 5 employees?
options: SELECT dept FROM Emp WHERE COUNT(*) > 5 GROUP BY dept;
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM Emp GROUP BY dept WHERE COUNT(*) > 5;
SELECT dept FROM Emp HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM Emp GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM Emp ORDER BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
questions.explanation: Group with GROUP BY, then filter groups with HAVING.

questions.question: A self join is used to:
options: Join two different tables that have no common columns
Return the Cartesian product of two tables
Remove duplicate rows from a table
questions.explanation: Self join = table joined with itself (e.g. employee and manager).

questions.question: Which statement about UNION ALL is correct?
options: It keeps duplicate rows and is generally faster than UNION
It returns only the common rows
It works only on tables with different structures
questions.explanation: No duplicate removal, so faster.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an aggregate function?
questions.explanation: UPPER() is a string (scalar) function.

questions.question: What is the output of SELECT ROUND(15.678, 1);?
questions.explanation: Rounded to 1 decimal place: 15.7.

questions.question: Which statement correctly creates an index on the name column of the Emp table?
options: CREATE TABLE INDEX idx_name ON Emp(name);
questions.explanation: CREATE INDEX name ON table(column).

questions.question: Which values does the condition WHERE marks BETWEEN 10 AND 20 include?
options: Values greater than 10 and less than 20 only
Both 10 and 20, and every value in between
questions.explanation: BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends.

questions.question: What is the output of SELECT SUBSTRING('DATABASE', 3, 4);?
questions.explanation: Start at position 3 (T), take 4 characters: TABA.

questions.question: Which condition correctly checks whether a column contains NULL?
questions.explanation: NULL is checked with IS NULL; = NULL never matches.

questions.question: A subquery returns multiple values. Which operator should be used in the WHERE clause to compare a column against those values?
questions.explanation: IN works with a list of values; = needs a single value.

questions.question: Which query lists the employees who earn more than the average salary?
options: SELECT * FROM Emp WHERE salary > AVG(salary);
SELECT * FROM Emp HAVING salary > AVG(salary);
SELECT AVG(salary) FROM Emp WHERE salary > salary;
SELECT * FROM Emp GROUP BY salary > AVG(salary);
SELECT * FROM Emp WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM Emp);
questions.explanation: Compute the average in a subquery.

questions.question: The salaries in a table are 500, 500, 400 and 300. Ordering by salary from highest to lowest, what rank does DENSE_RANK() assign to 300?
The ALTER TABLE command is used to:
options: Delete all rows from a table
Add, modify or drop columns in an existing table
questions.explanation: ALTER changes structure.

questions.question: A trigger in SQL is:
options: A stored program that runs automatically in response to an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE event
A function that must be called manually
A constraint that prevents NULL values
questions.explanation: Triggers fire automatically on events.

questions.question: Which statement about a standard (non-materialized) view is incorrect?
options: It can be used to restrict access to data
It always stores its own physical copy of the data
It is defined using a SELECT statement
questions.explanation: Only materialized/indexed views store data.

questions.question: A FULL OUTER JOIN returns:
options: Only the matching rows from both tables
All rows from the left table only
All rows from the right table only
The Cartesian product of both tables
All rows from both tables, with NULLs where there is no match
questions.explanation: Cartesian product is CROSS JOIN.

questions.question: Salaries are 900, 800, 800 and 700. Ordering from highest to lowest, what rank does RANK() assign to 700?
Which of the following statements about joins is incorrect?
options: An INNER JOIN returns only the matching rows
A LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table
A CROSS JOIN returns the Cartesian product
A NATURAL JOIN matches on columns that have the same name in both tables
A SELF JOIN requires two different tables
questions.explanation: A self join uses one table twice.

questions.question: Which keyword removes duplicate rows from the result of a SELECT query?
questions.explanation: SELECT DISTINCT.

questions.question: What is the correct order in which these clauses are written in a SELECT statement?
options: SELECT, WHERE, FROM, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY
SELECT, FROM, GROUP BY, WHERE, HAVING, ORDER BY
SELECT, FROM, WHERE, HAVING, GROUP BY, ORDER BY
SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY
SELECT, FROM, ORDER BY, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING
questions.explanation: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY.

questions.question: When there are tied values, ROW_NUMBER():
options: Assigns a unique sequential number to every row
Assigns the same number to each tied row
Leaves gaps in the sequence after ties
questions.explanation: ROW_NUMBER is always unique: 1, 2, 3...

questions.question: Which command removes a view from the database?
questions.explanation: DROP VIEW.

questions.question: A correlated subquery is one that:
options: Runs only once for the entire outer query
Is evaluated once for each row processed by the outer query
Can be used only in the FROM clause
questions.explanation: It references the outer row, so it re-runs per row. (a) describes a non-correlated subquery.

questions.question: What is the output of SELECT COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 5, 10);?
questions.explanation: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL value.

questions.question: In MySQL, which command renames a table?
options: UPDATE TABLE old SET NAME new;
questions.explanation: RENAME TABLE old TO new; (or ALTER TABLE old RENAME TO new;). SQL Server uses sp_rename.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraints is incorrect?
options: A table can have more than one UNIQUE constraint
A PRIMARY KEY column allows NULL values
A UNIQUE column allows NULL values
A PRIMARY KEY can be composite
questions.explanation: Primary keys never allow NULL.

questions.question: If no direction is specified, ORDER BY sorts results in:
questions.explanation: Default is ASC.

questions.question: Which operator returns only the rows that appear in the results of both queries?
questions.explanation: INTERSECT = common rows.

questions.question: In MySQL, which statement correctly creates a trigger that runs before a row is inserted into Emp?
options: CREATE TRIGGER trg BEFORE INSERT ON Emp FOR EACH ROW SET NEW.salary = 0;
CREATE TABLE trg BEFORE INSERT ON Emp;
TRIGGER trg ON Emp BEFORE INSERT;
CREATE VIEW trg BEFORE INSERT ON Emp;
questions.explanation: CREATE TRIGGER name BEFORE INSERT ON table FOR EACH ROW ...

questions.question: The REVOKE command is used to:
options: Remove privileges previously granted to a user
questions.explanation: REVOKE removes privileges (DCL).

questions.question: A column contains the values 10, 20, NULL and 30. What does AVG(column) return?
questions.explanation: NULL is ignored: (10 + 20 + 30) / 3 = 20.

questions.question: Which MySQL function returns the current date and time?
questions.explanation: NOW().

questions.question: Which query returns the second highest salary without using LIMIT?
options: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Emp WHERE salary > (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Emp);
SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Emp);
SELECT MIN(salary) FROM Emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Emp);
SELECT salary FROM Emp WHERE salary = MAX(salary) - 1;
questions.explanation: Highest value below the overall maximum.

questions.question: A stored procedure is:
options: A precompiled set of SQL statements stored in the database and called explicitly
A statement that runs automatically on every INSERT
questions.explanation: Procedures are called explicitly; triggers fire automatically.

questions.question: Which constraint provides a value for a column when no value is supplied during INSERT?
questions.explanation: DEFAULT.

questions.question: Which values does WHERE name LIKE '_a%' match?
questions.explanation: '_' = any one character, then 'a', then anything.

questions.question: Which relational algebra operator selects the rows that satisfy a given condition?
questions.explanation: σ = selection (rows). π = projection (columns).

questions.question: What does the projection operator (π) do?
options: Selects the specified columns of a relation
Selects rows based on a condition
Returns the common tuples of two relations
questions.explanation: π picks columns and removes duplicate rows.

questions.question: In Tuple Relational Calculus, which symbol expresses that at least one tuple satisfies a condition?
questions.explanation: ∃ = there exists. ∀ = for all.

questions.question: Compared with SQL, which operation cannot be performed directly in basic Tuple Relational Calculus?
questions.explanation: Basic TRC and RA can't aggregate (COUNT, SUM...).

questions.question: The division operator (÷) in relational algebra is used for queries involving:
questions.explanation: E.g. students who took ALL courses.

questions.question: Relation R has 3 tuples and relation S has 4 tuples. How many tuples does R × S contain?
questions.explanation: Cardinality of R × S = 3 × 4 = 12.

questions.question: Which statement about a B+ tree is correct?
options: All data pointers are stored in the leaf nodes, and the leaf nodes are linked together
Data pointers are stored only in the internal nodes
The leaf nodes are not linked to each other
questions.explanation: Linked leaves make range queries fast.

questions.question: A clustered index:
options: Can be created many times on the same table
Stores the index separately without reordering the data
Determines the physical order of the data rows, so a table can have only one
Is the same thing as a hash index
questions.explanation: One clustered index per table.

questions.question: A hash index is best suited for:
questions.explanation: Hash = exact match. B+ tree = ranges.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a B+ tree in databases?
questions.explanation: Efficient indexing (PYQ Prelims 2026).

questions.question: Which ACID property ensures that a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another while maintaining all defined rules?
questions.explanation: Consistency.

questions.question: After a crash, the log contains <Start T1>, <Commit T1> and <Start T2>. During recovery:
options: Both T1 and T2 are undone
Both T1 and T2 are redone
T1 is undone and T2 is redone
T1 is redone and T2 is undone
questions.explanation: Commit present (T1) = redo; no commit (T2) = undo.

questions.question: An account balance is 1000. A transaction runs these steps in order: add 200, then SAVEPOINT S1, then subtract 500, then ROLLBACK TO S1, then COMMIT. What is the final balance?
questions.explanation: Rollback to S1 undoes only the −500; +200 is committed.

questions.question: T1 and T2 both hold shared locks on item A. T3 now requests an exclusive lock on A. What happens?
options: T3 is granted the lock immediately
T1 and T2 are rolled back
The shared locks are upgraded automatically
T3 receives a shared lock instead
questions.explanation: X is incompatible with S.

questions.question: Which of the following queries is invalid?
options: SELECT dept FROM Emp WHERE AVG(salary) > 5000 GROUP BY dept;
SELECT dept, AVG(salary) FROM Emp GROUP BY dept;
SELECT dept FROM Emp GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(salary) > 5000;
SELECT dept FROM Emp WHERE salary > 5000 GROUP BY dept;
questions.explanation: Aggregates can't appear in WHERE.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C) has candidate key {A, B} and the functional dependency B → C. What is the highest normal form R satisfies?
questions.explanation: B is part of the key → partial dependency → only 1NF.

questions.question: In MySQL, which clause returns the 5th highest salary when salaries are ordered DESC?
questions.explanation: nth highest = LIMIT n-1, 1.

questions.question: Which of the following is a DDL command?
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE is DDL.

questions.question: Under the Wait-Die scheme, T2 (TS = 20) requests a lock held by T1 (TS = 10). What happens?
questions.explanation: T2 is younger (larger TS) and requests, so it dies.

questions.question: Which statement about a foreign key is incorrect?
options: It references the primary key or a unique key of another table
It must always be unique within its own table
questions.explanation: FKs don't need to be unique.

questions.question: Relation R(P, Q, R, S) has candidate key {P, Q} and the functional dependency Q → S. What is the highest normal form R satisfies?
questions.explanation: Q is part of the key → partial dependency → 1NF.

questions.question: Under Wait-Die, T1 (TS = 8) holds a lock and T3 (TS = 15) requests it. What happens?
questions.explanation: T3 is younger and requesting, so it dies.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: DROP removes both the table structure and its data
TRUNCATE removes all rows but keeps the structure
DELETE can use a WHERE clause
TRUNCATE is generally faster than DELETE
questions.explanation: DROP removes the structure too.

questions.question: A NATURAL JOIN matches rows using:
options: Columns that have the same name in both tables
Every column pair, producing a Cartesian product
A condition written in an ON clause
questions.explanation: Natural join uses same-named columns.

questions.question: Which relational algebra expression returns the names of employees whose salary is greater than 50,000?
questions.explanation: Read inside out: σ filters rows, then π picks the column.

questions.question: A foreign key is defined with ON DELETE CASCADE. When a parent row is deleted:
options: The child foreign keys are set to NULL
The matching child rows are also deleted
The child foreign keys are set to their default value
Nothing happens to the child rows
questions.explanation: CASCADE deletes the children too.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: Every relation in BCNF is also in 3NF
Every relation in 3NF is also in 2NF
BCNF requires every determinant to be a super key
3NF allows X → Y when Y is a prime attribute
Every relation in 3NF is always in BCNF
questions.explanation: 3NF ⇏ BCNF.

questions.question: Which constraint prevents duplicate values in a column but still allows NULLs?
questions.explanation: UNIQUE.

questions.question: In MySQL, what does SELECT INSTR('IBPS', 'Z'); return?
questions.explanation: INSTR returns 0 when not found (PYQ 2024).

questions.question: Money is debited from a sender's account, but a system failure stops it from being credited to the receiver. Which ACID property is violated?
questions.explanation: Atomicity.

questions.question: Under Wait-Die, T5 (TS = 30) holds a lock and T4 (TS = 12) requests it. What happens?
questions.explanation: T4 is older (smaller TS), so it waits.

questions.question: Under Wound-Wait, T6 (TS = 40) requests a lock held by T2 (TS = 10). What happens?
questions.explanation: T6 is younger; in Wound-Wait a younger requester waits.

questions.question: Which relational algebra expression returns the names of students in the 'IT' department?
questions.explanation: σ inside, π outside.

questions.question: In MySQL, what does SELECT INSTR('DATABASE', 'BASE'); return?
questions.explanation: D1 A2 T3 A4 B5: 'BASE' starts at 5.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has candidate key {A, B} and the functional dependencies AB → C and C → D. What is the highest normal form R satisfies?
questions.explanation: No partial dependency (C is outside the key), so 2NF. C → D is transitive, so not 3NF.

questions.question: Which statement about a clustered index is incorrect?
options: It determines the physical order of the rows
Searches on the clustered key are fast
In SQL Server, the primary key creates a clustered index by default
Range queries on the clustered key are efficient
A table can have several clustered indexes
questions.explanation: Only one clustered index per table.

questions.question: Which pair of commands are both DCL commands?
questions.explanation: DCL = GRANT, REVOKE.

questions.question: A 'lost update' occurs when:
options: New rows appear when a query is run again
Two transactions update the same item and one update overwrites the other
questions.explanation: Lost update. (a) = dirty read, (b) = phantom.

questions.question: Which join returns all rows from the right table plus the matching rows from the left table?
questions.explanation: RIGHT OUTER JOIN.

questions.question: Which ACID property ensures that committed changes are not lost after a system crash?
questions.explanation: Durability.

questions.question: T1 has TS = 50 and T2 has TS = 25. Which transaction is older?
questions.explanation: Smaller timestamp = started earlier = older.

questions.question: Under Wait-Die, T7 (TS = 5) requests a lock held by T8 (TS = 9). What happens?
questions.explanation: T7 is older, so it waits.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has candidate key {A, B} and the functional dependencies AB → C and AB → D only. What is the highest normal form R satisfies (considering functional dependencies only)?
questions.explanation: Every determinant is the key, so BCNF.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C) has candidate key A and the functional dependencies A → B and B → C. What is the highest normal form R satisfies?
questions.explanation: B → C is transitive, so 2NF.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: DROP removes the table's indexes and constraints along with the table
TRUNCATE can always be rolled back, regardless of the DBMS
TRUNCATE resets an identity/auto-increment counter in SQL Server and MySQL
questions.explanation: Whether TRUNCATE can be rolled back depends on the DBMS (PYQ 2024).

questions.question: In Tuple Relational Calculus, the symbol ∀ means:
options: There exists at least one tuple
questions.explanation: ∀ = for all.

questions.question: Which SQL feature performs calculations across a set of related rows while still returning each row individually, typically using PARTITION BY?
questions.explanation: Window function (PYQ 2024).

questions.question: What is the minimum isolation level that prevents dirty reads?
questions.explanation: 'Minimum' is the key word: Read Committed.

questions.question: Which type of index is best for the query WHERE emp_id = 1024?
options: A sparse index on unsorted data
questions.explanation: Equality search = hash index.

questions.question: Employee.manager_id references Employee.emp_id. To list each employee alongside their manager's name, you would use a:
questions.explanation: Same table joined to itself.

questions.question: What does SELECT name, salary, AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) FROM Emp; return?
options: One row per department containing its average salary
Only the employees whose salary is above average
Every employee row, along with the average salary of that employee's department
An error, because GROUP BY is missing
questions.explanation: Window functions keep every row and don't need GROUP BY.

questions.question: What is the minimum isolation level that prevents unrepeatable reads?
questions.explanation: Repeatable Read.

questions.question: Which index is best for the query WHERE salary BETWEEN 30000 AND 50000?
options: A sparse index on unsorted data
questions.explanation: Range query = B+ tree.

questions.question: Relation R(W, X, Y, Z) has candidate key {W, X} and the functional dependency W → Y. What is the highest normal form R satisfies?
questions.explanation: W is part of the key → partial dependency → 1NF.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C) has candidate key A and the functional dependencies A → B and A → C only. What is the highest normal form R satisfies?
questions.explanation: All determinants are the key, so BCNF.

questions.question: Under Wound-Wait, T9 (TS = 3) requests a lock held by T4 (TS = 7). What happens?
options: The lock is granted to both
questions.explanation: T9 is older and wounds the younger holder T4.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: WHERE is applied after GROUP BY
GROUP BY forms groups of rows that share values
questions.explanation: WHERE runs before GROUP BY.

questions.question: In relational algebra, the σ operator is used for:
options: Selecting rows that satisfy a condition
questions.explanation: σ = selection (rows).

questions.question: Which command is generally faster than DELETE for removing all rows, because it doesn't log each row individually?
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a checkpoint?
options: To reduce the work needed during crash recovery
questions.explanation: Checkpoint = faster recovery.

questions.question: Which data model organizes data in a tree (parent–child) structure, as used by IBM IMS?
questions.explanation: Hierarchical = tree, 1:N only. Network = graph (CODASYL).

questions.question: The relational model was proposed by:
questions.explanation: E.F. Codd, 1970. Peter Chen proposed the ER model (1976).

questions.question: Metadata ('data about data') is stored in the:
questions.explanation: Data dictionary / system catalog.

questions.question: The overall structure of a database that rarely changes is called the:
questions.explanation: Schema = structure; instance = data at a moment.

questions.question: The number of attributes (columns) in a relation is called its:
questions.explanation: Degree (arity) = columns; cardinality = rows.

questions.question: Which type of data independence is harder to achieve?
questions.explanation: Logical is harder, because apps depend on the logical structure.

questions.question: Which level of the three-schema architecture has exactly one schema for the whole database?
questions.explanation: One conceptual schema; many external views; one internal schema.

questions.question: Which of the following is a DDL command?
questions.explanation: DDL = CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME.

questions.question: In ER-to-table mapping, a 1:N relationship between two entities is usually implemented by:
options: Placing the FK on the N side
Placing the FK on the 1 side
Using a composite key on both tables
questions.explanation: No new table: FK goes on the many side. M:N needs a separate table.

questions.question: A multivalued attribute (e.g. several phone numbers) is mapped to:
questions.explanation: Multivalued attributes go into a separate table.

questions.question: Specialization is a ______ process, while generalization is a ______ process.
questions.explanation: Specialization: Employee → Manager/Engineer (top-down). Generalization: Car + Truck → Vehicle (bottom-up).

questions.question: A weak entity always has which type of participation in its identifying relationship?
questions.explanation: A weak entity can't exist without its owner, so participation is total.

questions.question: A system-generated key such as an IDENTITY or auto-increment column is called a:
questions.explanation: Surrogate key.

questions.question: A key made of two or more attributes is called a:
questions.explanation: Composite key.

questions.question: A minimal super key is called a:
questions.explanation: Candidate key = super key with no redundant attribute.

questions.question: Union, intersection and set difference require the two relations to be:
options: Union-compatible (same number of attributes with matching domains)
questions.explanation: Union-compatibility is required for set operations.

questions.question: R has 3 attributes and S has 4 attributes. What is the degree of R × S?
questions.explanation: Degree adds (3 + 4 = 7); cardinality multiplies.

questions.question: Which relational algebra operation is NOT commutative?
questions.explanation: R − S ≠ S − R.

questions.question: The rename operator in relational algebra is:
questions.explanation: ρ (rho) renames relations/attributes.

questions.question: According to Codd's theorem, relational algebra and safe relational calculus are:
questions.explanation: RA, safe TRC and safe DRC have the same expressive power.

questions.question: Relational calculus is a ______ query language.
questions.explanation: Calculus = what to get. Algebra = how to get it (procedural).

questions.question: Domain Relational Calculus uses variables that range over:
questions.explanation: DRC uses domain variables; TRC uses tuple variables.

questions.question: An index with an entry for every search-key value is a:
questions.explanation: Dense = every value; sparse = some values (needs sorted data).

questions.question: A sparse index can be used only when the data file is:
questions.explanation: Sparse indexes rely on the file being sorted.

questions.question: How many non-clustered indexes can a table have?
options: One per column only if it's a key
questions.explanation: Many non-clustered; only one clustered.

questions.question: Extendible hashing is an example of:
questions.explanation: Dynamic hashing lets the number of buckets grow.

questions.question: The search time in a B+ tree with n keys is:
questions.explanation: Balanced tree = O(log n).

questions.question: A transaction re-runs a query and finds new rows inserted by another transaction. This is a:
questions.explanation: Phantom read: new rows appear.

questions.question: A transaction reads the same item twice and gets different values because another transaction updated it in between. This is a(n):
questions.explanation: Unrepeatable read.

questions.question: Which intention lock signals that a transaction plans to take exclusive locks at a lower level?
questions.explanation: IX = intention exclusive. IS = intention shared.

questions.question: Which relationship between schedule classes is correct?
questions.explanation: Every strict schedule is cascadeless, and every cascadeless schedule is recoverable.

questions.question: Which statement is correct?
options: Conflict and view serializability are identical
Serializability has nothing to do with conflicts
Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable
Every view-serializable schedule is conflict serializable
questions.explanation: Conflict serializable ⊂ view serializable.

questions.question: The three phases of optimistic concurrency control are:
questions.explanation: Optimistic CC: work on local copies, validate, then write.

questions.question: In 2PL, upgrading a lock from S to X is allowed only during the:
questions.explanation: Acquiring/upgrading = growing; releasing/downgrading = shrinking.

questions.question: Which isolation level is SQL Server's default?
questions.explanation: SQL Server defaults to Read Committed.

questions.question: Under standard DBMS transaction theory, which command can generally be rolled back before COMMIT?
questions.explanation: DML (DELETE) can be rolled back; DDL is usually auto-committed (PYQ 2023).

questions.question: Which of the following is a NoSQL database?
questions.explanation: Cassandra (column-family). The rest are relational (PYQ 2022).

questions.question: In MongoDB, which feature ensures data availability in case of hardware failure?
questions.explanation: Replication = availability (PYQ 2023). Sharding = scaling.

questions.question: Redis is best described as a(n):
questions.explanation: Redis is an in-memory key-value store, often used for caching.

questions.question: According to the CAP theorem, a distributed system can guarantee at most:
options: Two of Consistency, Availability and Partition tolerance
questions.explanation: Only 2 of the 3.

questions.question: NoSQL systems typically follow which model instead of ACID?
questions.explanation: BASE: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent.

questions.question: In MongoDB terminology, a 'collection' corresponds to an RDBMS:
questions.explanation: Collection = table, document = row, field = column.

questions.question: NoSQL databases typically scale:
questions.explanation: NoSQL scales horizontally; RDBMS traditionally scales vertically.

questions.question: Log records needed to undo a transaction must be written before the data changes. This rule is called:
questions.explanation: WAL.
